lesson.title: Riding the X Chromosome: Sex-Linked Traits
lesson.summary: Genes located on the sex chromosomes, overwhelmingly the X, are inherited differently than genes on autosomes because males carry only a single copy and express whatever allele that one copy holds.
lesson.body:
A sex-linked gene is simply a gene that is physically located on one of the sex chromosomes rather than on one of the twenty two autosome pairs. In practice this almost always means the X chromosome. The Y chromosome is much smaller than the X and carries far fewer genes, most of them related to male sex determination itself, so the great majority of sex-linked traits studied in genetics are X-linked.

This location matters because males and females do not carry the same number of X chromosomes. A female, XX, carries two copies of every X-linked gene, just like she carries two copies of every autosomal gene, so she can be homozygous dominant, heterozygous, or homozygous recessive for an X-linked gene exactly as described in earlier chapters. A male, XY, carries only one X chromosome, so he carries only a single copy of every X-linked gene. Geneticists describe this situation as hemizygous: there is no second X-linked allele anywhere in his genotype that could potentially mask whatever allele is present on his one X.

The consequence follows directly from that difference. In a female, a single recessive X-linked allele is usually masked by a dominant allele sitting on her other X chromosome, so she is an unaffected carrier who can still pass the recessive allele on to her children. In a male, whatever single allele he happens to have inherited on his one X chromosome is expressed outright, whether it is dominant or recessive, because there is no second copy to override it. This is the underlying reason that recessive X-linked conditions show up noticeably more often in males than in females across a population.

That asymmetry is not just a rule to memorize, it is a direct, predictable outcome of combining hemizygosity with a Punnett square, and working through that math with a real human trait is exactly what the next chapter does.
